text: In bacterial transcription networks, negative autoregulation (NAR) — where a transcription factor represses its own gene — is the most common regulatory motif. Compared to an unregulated gene with the same steady-state level, what dynamical consequence does NAR have?
choices: Slower response time and increased cell-to-cell variability in protein levels
Bistability with two stable steady states and hysteresis
Faster response time to steady state and reduced cell-to-cell noise
Sustained oscillations with a period of approximately 24 hours
explanation: NAR speeds up the approach to steady state (roughly 2-fold for a Hill coefficient of 1) and reduces cell-to-cell variability, which is why it is the most common bacterial motif. Slower response and higher variability (choice 0) actually describe positive autoregulation, and bistability/hysteresis (choice 1) requires positive feedback with cooperativity, not negative feedback. A ~24-hour oscillation (choice 3) describes the circadian clock's delayed negative feedback loop, not a simple single-gene autoregulatory motif.
